title: Data analysis & SQL

options: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups
quiz.explain: WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY; HAVING filters the grouped results, e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5.

options: All left rows, with NULLs where there's no match
quiz.explain: LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table and fills right-side columns with NULL when nothing matches.
Use IS NULL.

quiz.prompt: Explain why COUNT(*) and COUNT(col) can differ.

Table and column constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, NOT NULL, UNIQUE)

quiz.explain: A foreign key ensures each referenced value exists in the parent table, so no orphan rows.
Normalising stores each fact once, so updates cannot leave contradictory copies behind.

quiz.prompt: A natural primary key is risky when:
quiz.explain: Keys get copied into other tables; if the real-world value (email, name) changes, every reference must change.

rubric: Avoid expensive joins on hot paths
Accept update complexity; keep a source of truth

covers: INSERT (single/multiple rows, from CSV), DELETE, UPDATE, triggers, soft deletions (L3 notes)
Views for simplifying, aggregating, partitioning, securing; CTEs; soft deletions with views (L4 notes)

practice.done_when: check50 green for all 4; running the loader twice leaves identical row counts.

options: Naming a subquery for readability and reuse
quiz.explain: A CTE names an intermediate result so a complex query reads top to bottom and can reuse it.
A normal view stores only its query text; it runs against the base tables each time you select from it.
An upsert (INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE in Postgres) inserts new rows and updates existing ones.

quiz.prompt: Why is an idempotent loader important for pipelines that may be retried?

Space and time trade-offs, partial indexes, VACUUM

quiz.prompt: An index speeds reads but costs:
quiz.explain: Every insert or update must also maintain each index, and indexes take disk space.
ACID = Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability; isolation controls what concurrent transactions see.
A sequential scan reads every row of the table; on a large table with a selective filter an index may help.

quiz.prompt: Why might Postgres ignore your index?

quiz.prompt: A window function differs from GROUP BY in that it:
options: Computes over related rows while keeping every row
quiz.explain: Window functions add a computed column (rank, running total) without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does.
timestamptz stores an absolute instant (normalised to UTC), avoiding timezone ambiguity.

options: JSONB stores parsed binary that can be indexed
quiz.explain: JSONB is stored decomposed in binary, supports GIN indexes and fast operators; JSON keeps the raw text.

quiz.prompt: When is JSONB the wrong choice vs proper columns?

quiz.explain: Parameters are sent separately from the SQL text, so input cannot change the query (no SQL injection).

options: The ordered schema changes applied to each DB
quiz.explain: Tools like Alembic keep an ordered, versioned list of schema changes and record which are applied.

options: The cost of opening a new connection per request
quiz.explain: A pool reuses open connections instead of paying the connect and auth cost on every request.

quiz.prompt: Why must schema changes be migrations rather than manual ALTERs on prod?

quiz.explain: Broadcasting stretches size-1 dimensions: (3,1) with (1,4) gives (3,4).
Basic slices share memory with the original array; modify the view and the original changes. Use .copy() if needed.
axis=0 sums down the rows, removing that axis and leaving one value per column: shape (3,).

Restarting clears all state, so running every cell in order proves the notebook works from scratch.
A Series is a single labelled column: values plus an index. A DataFrame is a table of Series.

quiz.explain: dropna() defaults to axis=0, how='any': it removes every row with at least one missing value.

options: Parquet is columnar, typed and compressed
quiz.explain: Parquet stores typed columns with compression, so it is smaller, faster to read and keeps dtypes.
Use df.loc[df.a > 0, 'b'] = 1.

quiz.prompt: Impute or drop? Give one case for each.
rubric: Drop: few rows, missing at random
Impute: many rows, simple/robust value or model

quiz.explain: how='left' keeps every row of the left frame, with NaN where the right frame has no match.
groupby splits rows by key and agg computes summaries per group, like SQL GROUP BY with aggregates.
A naive datetime has no tzinfo, so the instant it means is ambiguous; use aware datetimes.

quiz.prompt: To compare distributions across groups, prefer:
quiz.explain: Box/violin plots and histograms show spread and shape per group, not just a single number.
Two variables can move together because of a confounder or chance; correlation alone does not show cause.

quiz.prompt: The IQR outlier rule flags points beyond:
quiz.explain: Tukey's rule flags values more than 1.5×IQR below Q1 or above Q3.

quiz.explain: DuckDB runs inside your process (like SQLite) but is built for analytical, column-oriented queries.

options: Builds a query plan optimised on .collect()
quiz.explain: Lazy frames record operations, then optimise the whole plan (predicate pushdown etc.) when you call .collect().

quiz.prompt: OLTP vs OLAP: Postgres is primarily:
quiz.explain: Postgres is row-oriented and built for many small transactional reads and writes (OLTP).

quiz.prompt: When would you pick DuckDB over Postgres for an analysis?

options: Unexpected types, ranges and nulls before they reach consumers
quiz.explain: Validating schema and ranges at the boundary stops bad data before it silently breaks downstream jobs.

options: Where data came from and how it changed

options: Not necessarily licensed for your use

capstone.title: Messy data to trustworthy answers
capstone.brief: (12h) Take a messy public dataset (two related files, one with timestamps): Postgres schema via Alembic; idempotent Python loader with parameterised queries + upserts; 10 analytic SQL queries (≥3 with window functions or CTEs, EXPLAIN on one slow query + index); the same 3 answers in pandas or DuckDB with an equality test; EDA notebook (restart-and-run-all clean); pandera contract in CI; DATA_CARD.md + 1-page data-quality report. Pass ≥8/10.

rubric.criterion: SQL depth (joins, CTEs, windows, EXPLAIN + index)
levels: 2 – all, with an index improvement shown

rubric.criterion: Analysis honesty (cleaning log, missing-data decisions, limits)
